_doc: Field-wide milestones for the timeline (course-specific events live in each course.json). year < 0 means BC.

milestones.title: Medicine as observation
milestones.detail: The Hippocratic corpus treats disease as a natural event with natural causes, to be watched, recorded and reasoned about; the clinical history and the ethical tradition of the profession both descend from these writings.

milestones.title: Dissection at Alexandria
milestones.detail: Herophilos and Erasistratos dissect human bodies, distinguish arteries from veins, map the nerves and place intelligence in the brain rather than the heart.

milestones.title: Galen's synthesis
milestones.detail: Galen of Pergamum writes hundreds of books of anatomy, physiology and pharmacology from animals and from earlier authorities; his account of the body and of the humours dominates European medicine for fourteen centuries.

milestones.title: On the fabric of the human body
milestones.detail: Andreas Vesalius publishes De humani corporis fabrica on the basis of dissections he performed himself, correcting Galen where the human body differs from the animals Galen had cut, and founding descriptive anatomy on first-hand observation.

milestones.title: The circulation of the blood
milestones.detail: In a short book, De motu cordis, William Harvey calculates that the heart ejects far more blood in an hour than the body could make or consume, and concludes that blood is pumped in a closed circuit: the first quantitative argument in physiology.

milestones.title: The first microbes
milestones.detail: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek grinds his own lenses, examines scrapings from his own teeth and writes to the Royal Society in Delft about tiny moving 'animalcules': the first observations of bacteria.

milestones.title: A comparison of treatments at sea
milestones.detail: Aboard HMS Salisbury the ship's surgeon James Lind takes twelve scorbutic sailors, puts them in pairs and gives each pair a different supplement on top of the same diet; the two given citrus recover within days. The naval introduction of lemon juice follows half a century later.

milestones.title: Vaccination
milestones.detail: Edward Jenner inoculates eight-year-old James Phipps with material from a cowpox sore and later challenges him with smallpox, which does not take; his self-published inquiry of 1798 founds vaccination.

milestones.title: The stethoscope
milestones.detail: René Laennec, reluctant to put his ear to a young woman's chest, rolls paper into a tube and finds he hears the heart and lungs more clearly than by immediate auscultation; his treatise of 1819 turns the signs of chest disease into a system.

milestones.title: Sanitary reform by the numbers
milestones.detail: Edwin Chadwick reports on the sanitary condition of the labouring population of Britain, using death registration and local inquiries to show that drainage, water and housing determine how long people live; the report leads to the Public Health Act of 1848.

milestones.title: Childbed fever is carried on hands
milestones.detail: In the Vienna general hospital Ignaz Semmelweis makes students and doctors disinfect their hands with chlorinated lime before examining women in labour, after a colleague dies of the illness the women were dying of; mortality in his clinic falls sharply, and his evidence is rejected in his lifetime.

milestones.title: Taking the handle off the pump
milestones.detail: John Snow argues from the pattern of deaths in Soho that cholera is waterborne, and the Broad Street outbreak subsides after the pump handle is removed; his work founds outbreak investigation, and with Chadwick's the modern water and sewage services.

milestones.title: Disease lives in cells
milestones.detail: Rudolf Virchow's Cellular Pathology replaces the humours with the cell as the seat of disease, and gives medicine its vocabulary of hyperplasia, metaplasia, embolism and thrombosis.

milestones.title: Nursing as an occupation
milestones.detail: Using money raised after the Crimean War, where she had cut death rates by sanitary reform and by statistics she could put in front of politicians, Florence Nightingale opens a training school for nurses at St Thomas's Hospital in London.

milestones.title: Antisepsis
milestones.detail: Convinced by Pasteur that putrefaction is caused by living particles in the air, Joseph Lister dresses compound fractures with carbolic acid and reports in The Lancet a substantial fall in mortality; antiseptic, then aseptic, technique makes major surgery survivable.

milestones.title: One germ, one disease
milestones.detail: Robert Koch grows the anthrax bacillus in pure culture outside the animal, shows that it causes anthrax when injected into healthy mice and describes the resistant spore stage: experimental proof that a specific organism causes a specific disease, and the origin of Koch's postulates.

milestones.title: The tuberculosis bacillus
milestones.detail: Koch announces the identification of Mycobacterium tuberculosis; within a few years Edwin Klebs and Friedrich Löffler describe the diphtheria bacillus and Georg Gaffky the typhoid bacillus, and laboratory diagnosis of infection becomes routine.

milestones.title: A vaccine made in the laboratory
milestones.detail: Nine-year-old Joseph Meister, bitten by a rabid dog, is given a series of injections of attenuated rabies virus grown in rabbit spinal cord by Louis Pasteur and his team in Paris; he does not fall ill, and laboratory vaccines become a branch of medicine.

milestones.title: Serum therapy
milestones.detail: Emil von Behring and Kitasato Shibasaburō show that serum from animals immunised against diphtheria and tetanus transfers immunity and neutralises toxin in another animal: the first immunotherapy, and the work for which Behring receives the first Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1901.

milestones.title: Seeing inside the living body
milestones.detail: Investigating cathode rays in Würzburg, Wilhelm Röntgen finds a fluorescent screen glowing across the room and photographs the bones of his wife's hand; within a year X-rays are in hospitals, and the first radiation injuries are being described.

milestones.title: The synapse
milestones.detail: Santiago Ramón y Cajal's silver-stained sections establish that the nervous system is made of discrete cells rather than a continuous net, and Charles Scott Sherrington reasons that reflexes must cross a junction with properties of its own, which he names the synapse; Sherrington shares the 1932 Nobel Prize with Edgar Adrian.

milestones.title: Blood groups
milestones.detail: Karl Landsteiner finds that human sera agglutinate some red cell suspensions and not others, defining groups A, B and O, so that deaths from incompatible transfusion stop being an unexplained hazard; donation, storage and cross-matching follow.

milestones.title: Salvarsan, and chemotherapy
milestones.detail: Paul Ehrlich and Sahachiro Hata report the cure of experimental trypanosome infection and the treatment of syphilis with arsenical compound 606, marketed as Salvarsan: the idea that a chemical may be chosen for its selective toxicity to a pathogen.

milestones.title: Insulin
milestones.detail: Frederick Banting and Charles Best, with J. J. R. Macleod's laboratory at Toronto, obtain a pancreatic extract that lowers blood glucose in depancreatectomised dogs; after James Collip's purification patients begin treatment in January 1922, and juvenile diabetes changes from a fatal wasting disease into a manageable one.

milestones.title: Penicillin
milestones.detail: Returning from a holiday, Alexander Fleming finds that a staphylococcal plate left near an open window has been contaminated by a mould and that no colonies grow around it; he describes the diffusible antibacterial substance in mould filtrate as penicillin, and cannot get enough of it.

milestones.title: Penicillin in patients
milestones.detail: Howard Florey and Ernst Boris Chain, with Norman Heatley solving the production problem, carry penicillin from a curiosity to a medicine: the first patients treated at Oxford in 1941, a Medical Research Council trial against sulphonamides in war wounds, and large-scale manufacture in the United States.

milestones.title: Streptomycin, and the search in soil
milestones.detail: Albert Schatz, working in Selman Waksman's laboratory, obtains streptomycin from a soil actinomycete; it becomes the first reliable treatment for tuberculosis, and within a few years the first antibiotic whose usefulness is limited by resistance.

milestones.title: A world health organisation, and a controlled trial
milestones.detail: The constitution of the World Health Organization, with its definition of health as a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, comes into force on 7 April. In the same year the Medical Research Council reports its randomised trial of streptomycin plus bed rest against bed rest alone in pulmonary tuberculosis, the allocation designed by the statistician Austin Bradford Hill.

milestones.title: Smoking and lung cancer
milestones.detail: Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill publish a hospital-based comparison showing that carcinoma of the lung is very much commoner in smokers, and begin following some 40,000 British doctors prospectively; exposure, dose-response, latency and eventual decline are all in that one design.

milestones.title: The double helix; and the heart-lung machine
milestones.detail: James Watson and Francis Crick propose a base-paired structure for DNA, using Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling's X-ray diffraction photographs and Erwin Chargaff's base ratios; in the same year John Gibbon uses a mechanical heart and lungs to close an atrial septal defect in a patient who survives.

milestones.title: The first successful transplant
milestones.detail: At the Peter Bent Brigham Hospital Joseph Murray and J. Hartwell Harrison remove a kidney from one identical twin and place it in the other, where it works for eight years; transplantation is thereby defined as an immunological problem, and the era of immunosuppression begins.

milestones.title: Poliomyelitis vaccine
milestones.detail: Enders, Weller and Robbins have grown poliovirus in non-nervous tissue culture, and Jonas Salk's inactivated vaccine is tested in a field trial on schoolchildren larger than any before; licensure in April 1955 is followed by Albert Sabin's attenuated oral vaccine, which makes mass campaigns feasible.

milestones.title: Chest compression, and dialysis for life
milestones.detail: William Kouwenhoven, Guy Jude and James Knickerbocker report restoring circulation by external chest compression, the manoeuvre that makes resuscitation possible outside an operating theatre; in the same year Belding Scribner and Wayne Quinton fit a reusable vascular access so that patients with end-stage renal failure can be dialysed repeatedly rather than once.

milestones.title: A transplanted heart; and a determined eradication
milestones.detail: Christiaan Barnard transplants a heart at Groote Schuur hospital in Cape Town on 3 December. The same year the World Health Organization launches an Intensified Smallpox Eradication Programme, which with surveillance and ring vaccination rather than blanket coverage reaches the last natural case in 1977.

milestones.title: Computed tomography
milestones.detail: Godfrey Hounsfield at EMI, with the neurologist James Ambrose, reconstructs X-ray attenuation measured from many angles to display a slice of the living brain without opening the skull; computed tomography, and then magnetic resonance imaging, displace exploratory surgery in much of diagnosis.

milestones.title: Immunisation becomes a global programme
milestones.detail: The World Health Assembly establishes the Expanded Programme on Immunization so that children everywhere are protected against tuberculosis, diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus and measles, with poliomyelitis added later; its cold chain and coverage statistics become the backbone of child health.

milestones.title: Reading DNA
milestones.detail: Frederick Sanger develops chain-termination sequencing and, independently, Allan Maxam and Walter Gilbert a chemical degradation method; for the first time a gene can be read, and medical genetics moves from chromosomes and pedigrees to sequence.

milestones.title: Fertilisation outside the body
milestones.detail: Patrick Steptoe and Robert Edwards deliver Louise Brown by caesarean section in Oldham after fertilisation and early development in the laboratory; assisted reproduction becomes a specialty, and the embryo becomes a problem for medical ethics.

milestones.title: Smallpox eradicated
milestones.detail: The World Health Assembly declares that the world has won freedom from smallpox, more than three years after the last natural case in Somalia: the only human disease eradicated, and the template for the polio and guinea worm campaigns since.

milestones.title: An epidemic recognised; a retrovirus found
milestones.detail: In June the Centers for Disease Control report five cases of Pneumocystis pneumonia in previously healthy young men in Los Angeles, the first published account of what becomes AIDS; in 1983 Françoise Barré-Sinoussi and Luc Montagnier at the Institut Pasteur, and independently Robert Gallo's group, isolate the retrovirus now called HIV.

milestones.title: Amplifying DNA
milestones.detail: Kary Mullis describes the polymerase chain reaction, cycling denaturation, primer annealing and extension so that a minute quantity of DNA is copied into a detectable one; with a heat-stable polymerase from 1988 it becomes the ordinary instrument of diagnostic microbiology, transplant typing and forensic medicine.

milestones.title: A common genetic disease traced to a gene
milestones.detail: John Riordan, Lap-Chee Tsui, Francis Collins and colleagues identify the gene encoding the chloride channel CFTR as the cause of cystic fibrosis, the first disease gene found by moving along a chromosome from a linked marker; carrier testing, newborn screening and eventually drugs that correct the defective channel follow.

milestones.title: Gene therapy, and the genome project
milestones.detail: In September a four-year-old with severe combined immunodeficiency due to adenosine deaminase deficiency receives her own white cells modified with a normal copy of the gene at the US National Institutes of Health; in October Congress begins funding the Human Genome Project.

milestones.title: Evidence-based medicine
milestones.detail: The McMaster group led by Gordon Guyatt gives a name to a movement: the conscientious, explicit and judicious use of current best evidence in decisions about individual patients, combined with clinical expertise and the patient's values, with systematic review as its instrument; David Sackett's later formulation makes the triad canonical.

milestones.title: Tuberculosis control where care is scarce
milestones.detail: The World Health Organization adopts short-course chemotherapy with directly observed treatment, standardised recording and guaranteed drug supply, a strategy built on treatment studies in East Africa that had shown cure rates above 80% without expensive infrastructure; it remains the framework of global tuberculosis control.

milestones.title: A draft of the human genome
milestones.detail: The public Human Genome Project and a private consortium publish draft sequences of the human genome; the surprise is the small number of protein-coding genes, of the order of twenty thousand, which turns attention towards regulation, variation and non-coding DNA. The sequence is declared essentially complete in 2003 and gapless in 2022.

milestones.title: SARS, and global health security
milestones.detail: Carlo Urbani in Hanoi recognises that a severe respiratory illness in a patient who had travelled from Guangzhou is a new and transmissible pathogen and warns the World Health Organization, which issues a global alert on 12 March. The outbreak is contained by classic public health measures with genomic identification, and the International Health Regulations are revised in 2005.

milestones.title: Immunity unleashed; treatment as prevention
milestones.detail: Ipilimumab, an antibody that releases the CTLA-4 brake on T cells, is licensed for melanoma, beginning checkpoint inhibition in oncology; and a randomised trial shows that starting antiretroviral therapy early, while CD4 counts are still high, prevents most sexual transmission of HIV.

milestones.title: Ebola in West Africa
milestones.detail: The largest Ebola outbreak on record exposes how little intensive care, how few isolation wards and no licensed vaccine were available in the affected countries — and, in the event, how quickly a candidate vaccine could be manufactured and tested by ring vaccination in Guinea.

milestones.title: mRNA vaccines
milestones.detail: Vaccines using nucleoside-modified mRNA in lipid nanoparticles, resting on the work of Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman and on the BioNTech and Moderna platforms, are licensed against SARS-CoV-2 within about a year of the virus's sequence being released, and are given in billions of doses.

milestones.title: An approved gene-edited medicine
milestones.detail: A therapy that edits a patient's own blood stem cells at the erythroid enhancer of BCL11A, the repressor of fetal haemoglobin identified through work on inherited persistence of fetal haemoglobin, is licensed for severe sickle cell disease and transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia: gene editing becomes a prescription, written for one patient at a time.
